summary: Describes some theoretically possible failure modes for TCP connections, notably the hazards when a connection in the TIME-WAIT state receives a stray reset segment. It points out a very simple fix: ignore reset segments while in TIME-WAIT.

plainLanguage.summary: After a call ends, TCP waits a bit in case late messages arrive. A stray late message could hang up the next call by mistake. The fix is to ignore it.

subtitle: A security hazard where old duplicate TCP segments can prematurely close waiting connections.

tldr.problem: TCP's TIME-WAIT state is designed to protect against interference from old duplicate segments, but old duplicates can prematurely terminate TIME-WAIT through a mechanism called TIME-WAIT Assassination (TWA), exposing new connections to corruption.
tldr.mechanism: When a connection closes, TCP enters TIME-WAIT to let old segments expire. An old duplicate segment can trigger a reset that ends TIME-WAIT early, leaving the next connection vulnerable to accepting data from the old connection.
tldr.outcome: The simplest fix is to ignore reset segments while in TIME-WAIT state, which is the recommended solution to prevent the three identified hazards.

today: RFC 1337 is an Informational RFC that identified a real but unlikely vulnerability in TCP. The recommended fix (ignoring RST segments in TIME-WAIT) has been widely adopted in production TCP implementations, making the hazards described here extremely rare in modern networks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
TCP is the Internet's reliable transport protocol. When a TCP connection closes, it enters a special TIME-WAIT state that lasts about two minutes. This state protects against a classic problem: old duplicate segments (network packets) from the closed connection arriving late and interfering with a new connection between the same two hosts.

This RFC describes a vulnerability in that protection: old duplicate segments can prematurely end TIME-WAIT state through a process called TIME-WAIT Assassination (TWA), potentially exposing new connections to corruption, desynchronization, or failure.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP has a waiting period after closing to protect the next connection. But this RFC discovered that old stray messages can trick TCP into stopping the wait too early.

sections.title: How TIME-WAIT Protection Works
sections.content:
TCP prevents old duplicate segments from corrupting connections through several mechanisms. For new connections, the three-way handshake rejects duplicate initial packets. For ongoing connections, sequence numbers ensure old data and acknowledgments are ignored. The TIME-WAIT delay adds one more layer: after a connection closes, the closing end waits for 2 × MSL (maximum segment lifetime, typically 4 minutes) to allow any stray old segments time to disappear from the network before the connection can reopen.

The danger is that on high-speed or long-duration connections, sequence numbers can wrap around. If a new connection reuses the same source and destination addresses and ports, it might accept sequence numbers that actually belonged to an old segment. TIME-WAIT waits long enough for the old segments to naturally expire so they cannot interfere.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP has waiting periods and sequence numbers to make sure old messages do not mess up new calls between the same pair of computers. The TIME-WAIT period is the final safety net.

sections.title: TIME-WAIT Assassination Mechanism
sections.content:
An old duplicate segment arriving during TIME-WAIT state triggers TCP's half-open connection detection, designed to clean up after system crashes. The receiving end sends an acknowledgment for its current state. The other end, which has no record of this connection, responds with a reset (RST) segment. This RST terminates TIME-WAIT prematurely, assassinating the waiting state before old segments have expired.

Figure 1 of the RFC shows this sequence: a closed connection lingers in TIME-WAIT, then an old duplicate data segment arrives, triggering an acknowledgment, which provokes a reset that immediately closes TIME-WAIT and returns the connection to CLOSED state. The assassination is not an unlikely accident if the network occasionally duplicates packets; it is a natural consequence of TCP's design.
sections.plainLanguage: When a stray old message arrives during the wait, TCP tries to figure out if it is a forgotten connection coming back to life. This triggers a reset that kills the wait, even though the wait was supposed to keep running.

sections.title: The Three Hazards of Premature Closure
sections.content:
If TIME-WAIT ends prematurely and a new connection immediately reopens between the same hosts and ports, three failure modes become possible. Hazard H1: old duplicate data from the earlier incarnation might fall within the receive window of the new connection, causing the application to accept corrupted data. Hazard H2: a stray old acknowledgment could cause the two ends to fall permanently out of sync, leading to an infinite loop of corrective acknowledgments. Hazard H3: an old reset segment might arrive during the new connection's setup phase and kill it prematurely.

The RFC demonstrates that all three hazards are theoretically possible through examples and notes they have been reproduced in laboratory conditions. However, they require the unfortunate coincidence of a duplicate segment arriving at exactly the right time in the sequence space of the new connection, so they are much less probable than TIME-WAIT Assassination itself.
sections.plainLanguage: When the wait ends too early, three bad things could happen to the next call: the wrong old message gets delivered, both ends get confused and argue forever, or a stray reset kills the new call.

sections.title: Proposed Solutions and Recommendations
sections.content:
The RFC discusses three possible fixes. Fix F1 (recommended): simply ignore all reset segments while in TIME-WAIT state. Since TIME-WAIT exists to let old segments expire, it makes sense that it should not be ended by a reset. This is the simplest fix and prevents all three hazards if the 2-minute TIME-WAIT delay is enforced. Fix F2: use PAWS (Protect Against Wrapped Sequences) timestamps to allow resetting based on whether timestamp clocks have advanced far enough. This is more complex and only partially solves the problem; old duplicate acknowledgments can still slip through. Fix F3: expand TCP sequence numbers from 32 to 64 bits, making it so connections are always "short and slow" and do not need TIME-WAIT for protection. This would be a major protocol change.

The RFC concludes that F1 is the best short-term solution due to its simplicity and effectiveness. The authors recommend testing this fix in production networks to ensure ignoring RSTs in TIME-WAIT has no unexpected side effects.
sections.plainLanguage: Fix 1: ignore reset messages during the wait. Fix 2: use timestamps to decide when it is safe to reset. Fix 3: use much bigger sequence numbers so you never need a wait. The RFC says Fix 1 is best and easiest.

items.title: H1: Bad Data
items.text: Old data from previous connection accepted.

items.title: H2: Desync
items.text: Ends disagree on state, infinite ACK loop.

items.title: H3: Connection Dies
items.text: Old reset kills new connection during setup.
